caption: A map for following how a choice takes shape. The steps can overlap or repeat; green arrows show how learning can influence later decisions.
attributes: #fig-master-loop fig-alt="Context and information lead into notice and interpret; construct options; predict consequences; value consequences; choose and commit; and observe and learn. One shared green return path branches into the five decision functions before observation and learning. It has no direct arrow to the current inputs. An enclosing frame shows that people, institutions, and design can shape the whole process. The map organizes questions rather than specifying a fixed psychological sequence." .phone-fit

caption: A normative decision process built around the rational-choice benchmark. Information about alternatives supports prediction; prediction informs valuation; valuation supports choice; and outcomes can provide feedback for later judgment.
attributes: #fig-normative-decision-loop fig-alt="A normative decision loop. Information about alternatives enters a judgment box containing prediction followed by valuation. Valuation supports choice, choice leads to an outcome, and feedback from the outcome can inform later judgment."

caption: How decisions are made. External context shapes presented information and the decision-maker's internal state and model. Within judgment, selection and interpretation interact with prediction and valuation. Judgment supports choice and action; outcomes provide feedback that may update, reinforce, or fail to correct the internal model.
attributes: #fig-behavioral-decision-loop fig-alt="A behavioral decision loop. External context shapes presented information and the decision-maker's internal state and model. Within judgment, selection and interpretation have two-way connections with prediction and valuation. Judgment supports choice and action, choice leads to an outcome, and feedback may update the internal model."

caption: Two lecture experiments (Sana et al., 2013). A: laptop note-taking with or without unrelated online tasks (20 students per group). B: paper note-taking with or without a view of multitasking laptops (19 per group). Bars show means; error bars are standard errors calculated from rounded reported standard deviations. Conditions differed between experiments, so their effect sizes should not be compared directly.
attributes: #fig-laptop-distraction .phone-fit fig-alt="Two separate experiments compare average comprehension scores. In the first, laptop note takers scored 66 percent without additional online tasks and 55 percent with them. In the second, paper note takers scored 73 percent without a view of multitasking laptops and 56 percent with a view. Error bars show standard errors."

caption: Attention selects and prioritizes information for conscious report and deliberate use.
attributes: #fig-attention-filter fig-alt="Many information streams compete for selection. Goals, salience, expectations, and load influence which signals become consciously reportable and deliberately usable. Unselected information may still receive limited processing."

caption: Four sensory worlds: infrared, ultraviolet, infrasound, and geomagnetic cues.
attributes: #fig-sensory-windows fig-alt="Four pencil-style scenes show a pit viper sensing infrared radiation from a warm mouse with its facial pit; a bee beside matched flowers in visible light and false-colour ultraviolet, revealing a dark petal-base pattern; Asian elephants with low-frequency sound waves; and a European robin beside schematic geomagnetic field lines." .wide-illustration

caption: What do these patches represent? Record your first impression before continuing.
attributes: #fig-recognition-two-tone fig-alt="Irregular black patches on a white field. Some form small isolated clusters, while others join into larger dark regions. The image's subject is deliberately left unnamed for this recognition exercise." width=100% .phone-fit

caption: An original perceptual-context demonstration uses exactly the same middle vector mark in two rows. Number context invites a reading of “13,” while letter context invites a reading of “B.”
attributes: #fig-context-b13-demonstration fig-alt="Two horizontal rows contain the same central ambiguous mark. The top row places it between 12 and 14, encouraging a reading of 13. The bottom row places it between A and C, encouraging a reading of B." width=100%

caption: A line drawing can be read as a duck facing right or a rabbit facing left. The two long extensions become a bill in one interpretation and ears in the other.
attributes: #fig-duck-rabbit-context fig-alt="A single navy outline on white has a shared eye, rounded head, and two long extensions pointing right. It can be interpreted as a duck facing right, with the extensions forming its bill, or as a rabbit facing left, with the extensions forming its ears." width=100% .phone-fit

caption: Three perceptual demonstrations hold a measurable target constant while changing its context: equal line shafts receive different fins, equal centre circles receive differently sized neighbours, and identical grey patches appear on dark and light fields.
attributes: #fig-perception-context-lab fig-alt="Three panels compare physically identical targets in different contexts. Equal horizontal shafts have different arrow fins, equal blue centre circles are surrounded by small or large circles, and identical grey patches appear on dark and light backgrounds. Each panel states the physical equality." width=100%

caption: The same gray lens appears alone on a blue-green field and at the top of a familiar traffic signal. The housing, other lamps, and street scene provide context only on the right.
attributes: #fig-traffic-light-color-context fig-alt="The left panel contains only a gray textured lens on a plain blue-green background, with no frame or other objects. The right places the identical lens at the same size and height at the top of a three-lamp traffic signal in a blue-green scene. The familiar upper position supplies the learned expectation of red." width=100% .phone-fit

caption: A simplified predictive-processing account. Expectations and incoming signals both contribute to perception; action changes subsequent sampling, while mismatches can update the model. Estimated reliability affects the weight given to the signals.
attributes: #fig-predictive-processing-decision fig-alt="Expectations and incoming signals converge on perception. Perception informs action and sampling, which changes the next evidence. A feedback arrow shows that mismatch can update the internal model."

caption: The grayscale source of the opening image. Compare the same landmarks in both versions, then try to recover your first impression of the patches.
attributes: #fig-recognition-grayscale fig-alt="A grayscale illustration of a Dalmatian resting in dappled shade, its head facing left. Its nose is near the center-left, its eye is above it, and a dark ear hangs on the right." width=100% .phone-fit

caption: Expectations can affect outcomes through four parallel pathways: physiological response, the person's behavior, other people's responses, and the allocation of resources or opportunities. Feedback may reinforce the expectation in a self-fulfilling pattern or counteract the predicted outcome in a self-defeating pattern.
attributes: #fig-expectation-loop fig-alt="An expectation branches into four parallel pathways: physiological response, behavior and effort, other people's responses, and resources and opportunities. The pathways converge on changed outcomes and evidence. A feedback path distinguishes self-fulfilling reinforcement from self-defeating prevention."

caption: Four groups make the influences on value easier to inspect: the option, current state, goals and experience, and social meaning.
attributes: #fig-valuation fig-alt="Four groups of possible influences converge on current value: the option and comparisons, current state, goals and experience, and social meaning. Current value can guide motivation and choice."

caption: Overlapping motive systems across development. Earlier-developing systems remain available as later systems emerge. The arrangement follows their proposed developmental emergence.
attributes: #fig-overlapping-motive-systems fig-alt="A pile of seven complete, overlapping triangles shows proposed motive systems. From the broadest triangle upward, they are immediate physiological needs, self-protection, affiliation, status and esteem, mate acquisition, mate retention, and kin care. The exposed diagonal edges show that later-developing systems are added without removing earlier systems. A developmental guide labels the direction from earlier to later emergence."

caption: A choice-blindness switch: face A is selected, but face B is returned and presented for explanation. If the switch is unnoticed, reasons may be offered for the rejected face. The portraits are fictional illustrations, not the original experimental stimuli.
attributes: #fig-choice-blindness-swap .phone-fit fig-alt="Three stages use two distinct illustrated faces. Face A, with long dark hair, is selected over face B, with short auburn hair. The cards are covertly exchanged. Face B is then returned with the question why did you choose this face." width=640

caption: A contemporaneous decision record provides an independent comparison for detecting hindsight and outcome-based rewriting.
attributes: #fig-narrator-learning fig-alt="Choice leads to outcome, narrative, and a future rule, while a contemporaneous decision record provides an independent comparison for detecting hindsight."

caption: A heuristic often answers an easier question than the one the decision actually requires.
attributes: #fig-heuristic-substitution fig-alt="A target question is replaced by an easier question and then produces a quick answer." .phone-fit

caption: System 1 and System 2 name families of processes, not separate brain structures. Automatic processes often supply candidate answers; working-memory-dependent processes can sometimes inspect, inhibit, redirect, or train them.
attributes: #fig-fast-slow fig-alt="Two columns summarize System 1 and System 2 processing features. System 1 is typically fast, automatic, low effort, associative, and cue driven. System 2 is typically working-memory dependent, effortful, rule guided, and capable of hypothetical reasoning. Arrows show candidate answers and possible inspection or training." .phone-fit

caption: Counting on fingers makes an arithmetic procedure visible. With suitable practice and feedback, the answer may later be retrieved without counting.
attributes: #fig-daughter-finger-counting fig-alt="A three-year-old child looks down at her hands while counting on her fingers to work out four plus one." width=42% fig-align="center"

caption: A self-contained Stroop activity. Neutral strings carry ink colour without a competing colour name; incongruent colour words add a practised, task-irrelevant reading response.
attributes: #fig-stroop-interference-lab fig-alt="Two large rows ask the reader to name ink colour. The neutral row contains red, blue, green, and orange strings of X characters. The conflict row contains colour words printed in incongruent colours." width=100%

caption: A giant panda cub and ochre sea stars invite a comparison of immediate emotional appeal.
attributes: #fig-affect-panda-sea-star fig-alt="A fluffy giant panda cub rests its tilted head against a tree fork and hugs the branch. Beside it, purple and orange ochre sea stars with thick, textured arms cling to wet intertidal rocks among mussels and algae. Both scenes receive equal visual space; the illustration provides no evidence about their relative conservation value." width="88%"

caption: Affect and availability become biases when a feeling or memorable case silently substitutes for probability and evidence.
attributes: #fig-affect-availability fig-alt="Affect and available examples converge on a substituted judgment, followed by a denominator and reference-class audit."

caption: A category resemblance can suggest a hypothesis; updating its probability requires the prior and evidence that distinguishes competing explanations.
attributes: #fig-prototype-probability fig-alt="Two paths are contrasted. The representativeness heuristic produces an impression from similarity; a probability update combines the prior probability with how likely the evidence is under the competing explanations." .phone-fit

caption: Selective search, interpretation, memory, and confidence can reinforce an existing belief.
attributes: #fig-belief-protection-loop fig-alt="Selective search, interpretation, memory, and confidence form a reinforcing loop, with disconfirming tests and independent standards as interventions."

caption: Two distinct empirical patterns. Anchoring means that an available number can shift a later estimate toward it; insufficient adjustment and selective accessibility are among several proposed mechanisms. The attraction effect means that adding an asymmetrically dominated decoy can increase the choice share of the option that dominates it.
attributes: #fig-anchor-decoy fig-alt="The anchoring panel separates the observed shift toward an available number from four possible mechanisms: insufficient adjustment, selective accessibility, scale use, and conversational inference. The attraction-effect panel shows options A and B, then an inferior decoy B-minus, and states that adding the decoy can increase B's choice share."

caption: A reported classroom demonstration of the subscription decoy effect. With a dominated print-only option in the menu, 16 of 100 participants chose web only, none chose print only, and 84 chose print plus web. In a different group shown only the two target options, 68 chose web only and 32 chose print plus web. Classroom choice counts reported by Ariely (2008).
attributes: #fig-subscription-decoy fig-alt="Two side-by-side subscription menus show reported choices in classroom groups of 100. With a print-only decoy priced at 125 dollars, 16 chose web only at 59 dollars, none chose print only at 125 dollars, and 84 chose print plus web at 125 dollars. Without the decoy, 68 chose web only and 32 chose print plus web."

caption: The selected view and the imagined whole. Each upper frame repeats exactly the corresponding frame and view below. Pale surroundings above show possible reconstructions that go beyond the information inside the frame.
attributes: #fig-framing-three-windows fig-alt="Below, three identical wooden frames select buildings, a park, and a leaking hydrant from one neighborhood. Above, the same frames and their contents are repeated without change against pale imagined surroundings: a dense city, an extensive park, and a flooded street. The selected information is unchanged; the imagined whole depends on which part is selected." width=100% .wide-illustration

caption: Two questions make different options salient. “Do you want an egg?” keeps no and yes visible, whereas “Would you like one egg or two?” makes eating implicit and asks only about quantity.
attributes: #fig-assumed-choice-eggs fig-alt="Two side-by-side menu panels. The first asks whether the person wants an egg and displays no and yes. The second asks whether the person wants one or two eggs and displays only one and two. The second question makes adding an egg implicit." width=100%

caption: Question wording changed both immediate speed estimates and later reports of nonexistent broken glass. Published values from Loftus and Palmer (1974).
attributes: #fig-wording-memory-study-redraw fig-alt="A two-panel original chart. In Experiment 1, with 45 students in five groups of nine, mean speed estimates rise from 31.8 miles per hour for contacted to 40.8 for smashed. In Experiment 2, with 50 students per group, 32 percent of the smashed group reported broken glass versus 14 percent of the hit group and 12 percent of controls, although no broken glass appeared."

caption: What lies outside the frame matters. Similar green views can belong to an extensive park or a small park surrounded by buildings; the narrow view alone cannot establish the larger context.
attributes: #fig-framing-view-and-context fig-alt="Two imagined settings contain similar framed views of a green path with trees and benches. The upper frame sits in an extensive park; the lower frame sits in a smaller green space surrounded by tall apartment buildings. The contrast is in the surroundings outside the frames." width=100% .phone-fit

caption: An earlier cue can make a meaning more accessible, which may influence how the next input is understood. The input itself remains a separate source of evidence.
attributes: #fig-priming-pathway fig-alt="An earlier cue makes a meaning easier to retrieve. The accessible meaning and the current input converge on interpretation."

caption: Repetition, clarity, familiarity, and pronounceability can alter processing ease. Ease can influence perceived truth, liking, confidence, and judgments of risk or safety.
attributes: #fig-fluency-pathway fig-alt="Four possible sources—repetition, clarity, familiarity, and pronounceability—converge on processing ease. Ease can influence perceived truth, liking, confidence, or context-specific risk and safety judgment. A separate evidence check asks what caused the ease and what independent evidence supports the inference." .phone-fit

caption: A positive result can come from either group. In this hypothetical population, the much larger group without disease supplies most of the positive tests.
attributes: #fig-probability-judgment-map fig-alt="A natural-frequency tree starts with 10,000 people: 100 have the disease and 9,900 do not. With ninety-percent sensitivity, 90 people with disease test positive. With a nine-percent false-positive rate, 891 people without disease test positive. Therefore 90 of the 981 positive tests, about 9.2 percent, come from people with disease." width=100%

caption: A teaching simulation of 50 measurement pairs illustrates regression to the mean. With a correlation near 0.40, an initial result two standard deviations above average predicts a second result only 0.8 standard deviations above average. The optional analysis gives the simulation specification.
attributes: #fig-regression-conditional-shrinkage fig-alt="A fixed-seed simulation of 50 standardized measurement pairs has an approximately 0.40 sample correlation under a declared normal data-generating process. The conditional prediction line is flatter than the no-noise identity line. Guides show that an initial value two standard deviations above average predicts a second value 0.8 standard deviations above average." width=100%

caption: As information accumulated, confidence rose without a corresponding gain in accuracy (Oskamp, 1965, Table 2). Thirty-two judges answered the same 25 five-option questions at four information stages about one case. Lines connect reported stage means.
attributes: #fig-confidence-accuracy fig-alt="Across four information stages, mean confidence is 33.2, 39.2, 46.0, and 52.8 percent; mean accuracy is 26.0, 23.0, 28.4, and 27.8 percent. Distinct lines and markers distinguish confidence from accuracy." .phone-fit

caption: The standard Monty Hall protocol keeps the information-generating rule visible. The initial choice has probability one-third, the two unchosen doors carry two-thirds together, and a knowledgeable host must reveal a goat before offering a switch, using a random tie-break when either goat door is available. The remaining unchosen door retains the two-thirds branch.
attributes: #fig-monty-hall-protocol fig-alt="Three stages show a Monty Hall problem. First, the chosen door receives one-third probability and the two unchosen doors receive two-thirds together. Second, a knowledgeable host opens an unchosen goat door under a constrained rule, choosing randomly when either goat door could be opened. Third, keeping retains one-third while switching receives two-thirds." width=100%

caption: A 50–50 lottery paying 0 or 100 has expected value 50. Under an illustrative square-root utility function, expected utility is 5, the certainty equivalent is 25, and the risk premium is 25. A companion panel separates known risk from ambiguous probabilities and shows why the process should be assessed using information available before the outcome.
attributes: #fig-risky-decision-map fig-alt="Two-panel diagram. The left panel plots a concave square-root utility curve from wealth zero to one hundred, marks lottery outcomes zero and one hundred, shows expected value fifty, expected utility five, certainty equivalent twenty-five, and risk premium twenty-five. The right panel contrasts a transparent known-risk urn with an ambiguous urn, then shows a process arrow leading to multiple possible outcomes to emphasize that a good decision can lose and a poor decision can win." width=100%

caption: Schematic curves illustrate prospect theory’s S-shaped value function around a reference point and inverse-S probability-weighting function. Under commonly used parameterizations, they can produce the fourfold pattern: caution for high-probability gains and low-probability losses, but risk seeking for low-probability gains and high-probability losses.
attributes: #fig-prospect-theory-map fig-alt="Three-part diagram. The left panel shows a value function centered at a reference point: concave for gains, convex and steeper for losses. The right panel shows an inverse-S probability-weighting curve relative to the forty-five-degree objective-probability line, emphasizing possibility and certainty. The bottom panel is a four-cell table mapping high- and low-probability gains and losses to typical risk attitudes and examples." width=100%

caption: Four information states created by the presence or absence of statistical description and personal experience.
attributes: #fig-decision-experience-states fig-alt="A two-by-two matrix. Columns indicate description absent or present; rows indicate experience absent or present. Neither is labeled information-poor. Description only means an explicit model without personal feedback; experience only means a sampled path without an explicit distribution; both means evidence sources can reinforce or conflict."

caption: An independently occurring rare event can remain absent from a small experience sample. With 15 observations, a 1% event remains unseen about 86% of the time and a 5% event about 46% of the time. The highlighted band shows a small sample of 11–19 observations for comparison.
attributes: #fig-experience-rare-event-sampling fig-alt="Line chart showing the probability that a rare event has not appeared after up to one hundred independent observations. The one-percent-event curve falls slowly and the five-percent-event curve falls more quickly. A band marks sample sizes eleven to nineteen. A side panel reports that at fifteen observations a one-percent event is absent with probability eighty-six percent and a five-percent event is absent with probability forty-six percent." width=100%

caption: Mental accounting can label, code, bracket, couple, or close outcomes before valuation. The resulting boundaries may support an endorsed goal or distort substitution across otherwise-equivalent resources.
attributes: #fig-mental-accounting-map fig-alt="An outcome enters a box of possible mental-accounting operations: label or open an account, code or post an outcome, bracket outcomes, and couple consumption with payment or close an account. A valuation layer compares the representation with a reference point. Two arrows show that a boundary may support a goal or distort substitution."

caption: Two studies offer different kinds of evidence about investment decisions. In Odean's (1998) brokerage sample, winners sold outperformed losing positions retained by about 3.41 percentage points in market-adjusted return over the following year. In Study 3 of Benartzi and Thaler (1999), median hypothetical stock allocations were 40% when staff saw one-year return distributions and 90% when they saw 30-year distributions (25 participants per group).
attributes: #fig-mental-accounting-evidence-redraw fig-alt="Two-panel comparison. The left panel contrasts a winner sold with a loser held and reports a 3.41-percentage-point difference in subsequent market-adjusted return, with a forward-looking question asking whether the investor would buy the position today. The right panel shows median hypothetical stock allocations of forty percent under annual return distributions and ninety percent under thirty-year distributions, with twenty-five participants in each group." width=100%

caption: Three discount models illustrate different implications. With linear utility, the quasi-hyperbolic example prefers €120 in thirteen months when viewed today but reverses to €100 when that reward becomes immediate; exponential discounting keeps the relative ranking stable. The optional analysis specifies the plotted functions and parameters.
attributes: #fig-discount-model-crossover fig-alt="A plot compares exponential, hyperbolic, and quasi-hyperbolic discount functions with declared parameters. Below it, a worked quasi-hyperbolic example prefers 120 euros in thirteen months when both rewards are delayed but reverses to 100 euros when the smaller reward becomes immediate. A note says the exponential example remains time consistent." width=100%

caption: Intertemporal choice can be shaped by immediate salience, uncertainty, weak future imagery, friction, and changing states.
attributes: #fig-intertemporal-choice fig-alt="An author's diagnostic synthesis shows two paths from a choice point. Possible bottlenecks on a delayed path include uncertainty, weak future imagery, and friction; design levers can be tested against them."

caption: The abbreviated and complete-stream displays contain the same payoffs. Writing the otherwise hidden zeros makes the forgone outcome at each date explicit and can redirect attention to opportunity cost.
attributes: #fig-hidden-zero-frame fig-alt="Two panels show the same intertemporal payoffs. The abbreviated panel displays 100 euros today or 120 euros in one month and leaves the other dates unstated. The complete panel displays 100 euros today plus zero next month, or zero today plus 120 euros next month." width=100%

caption: CIAO: following a routine. The dashed arrow marks a later encounter with the cue.
attributes: #fig-habit-loop fig-alt="Four equal segments form a ring: Cue, Impulse, Action, and Outcome. Three solid clockwise arrows trace an episode in that order. A dashed arrow from Outcome to Cue marks a later encounter with the cue. Learning across repetitions appears in the center." .phone-fit

caption: A schematic rise in automaticity. The vertical dotted line marks the time to reach the habit line at 95% of the plateau.
attributes: #fig-habit-formation-curve fig-alt="An automaticity curve crosses a horizontal dashed habit line at 95% of the plateau, labeled on the right. A vertical dotted line runs from the crossing to the time axis." width=100% fig-align="center" style="max-width: 560px !important;" .phone-fit

caption: Reward prediction error: schematic changes in dopamine-neuron firing. A: the cue does not yet predict reward, so the burst occurs at reward. B: a learned cue predicts reward. C: an expected reward is omitted. D: reward arrives later than expected. Zero represents baseline dopamine-neuron firing (Schultz et al., 1997; Hollerman & Schultz, 1998).
attributes: #fig-reward-prediction-error-shift fig-alt="Four panels show schematic changes in dopamine-neuron firing over time. A stays at baseline after a cue that does not yet predict reward, then rises at the unexpected reward. B rises at the learned cue and shows little additional response at reward. C rises at the cue and falls below baseline when reward is omitted. D rises at the cue, dips when reward was due, and rises again when the delayed reward arrives. Baseline does not mean no dopamine." .phone-fit width=98%

caption: Certain versus uncertain reward. The dashed blue curve represents a 50% chance of reward and shows sustained anticipatory activity during the waiting period. At the outcome, firing briefly rises above baseline if reward appears (green) or dips below baseline if it is omitted (red). Zero represents baseline dopamine-neuron firing. Curves are schematic (Fiorillo et al., 2003).
attributes: #fig-reward-uncertainty-comparison fig-alt="A solid teal line represents certain reward; a dashed blue line represents a 50% reward probability before the outcome. The certain cue elicits a larger brief response, followed by activity near baseline. The uncertain condition includes a smaller cue response and sustained activity increasing toward the outcome. At the outcome, a green dashed branch rises if reward is received, while a red dashed branch falls if it is omitted. Both branches share the same pre-outcome path. Curves show schematic changes in firing around baseline, not absolute dopamine release." .phone-fit width=98%

caption: A schematic course of urge intensity, with no fixed timescale. Urges can persist or return.
attributes: #fig-urge-wave-observation fig-alt="A schematic curve of urge intensity rises to a rounded peak and then gradually declines. The line changes from yellow through orange to red around the peak, then through purple and blue to green as intensity declines. The axes have no numerical scale." width=100% .phone-fit

caption: Six perspectives connect a choice to experience, memory, and judgments about life.
attributes: #fig-well-being-six-lenses fig-alt="Four stations follow a choice through time: predicted utility before the choice, decision utility when choosing, experienced utility during the outcome, and remembered utility afterward. Each has a short guiding question. A separate band across the bottom contains life evaluation and meaning and purpose, representing broader perspectives rather than a final stage."

caption: The two cold-water protocols and the subsequent repeat choice (Kahneman et al., 1993). Temperatures are nominal; the added interval remained painful. The strips show timing, not pain ratings.
attributes: #fig-cold-water-better-ending fig-alt="The short trial lasts 60 seconds at 14 degrees Celsius. The long trial has the same first minute, followed by 30 seconds during which the water gradually warms toward 15 degrees Celsius. Twenty-two of 32 analyzed participants chose to repeat the longer trial." .phone-fit

caption: Schematic income–well-being patterns: how our understanding evolves over time.
attributes: #fig-income-wellbeing-evidence-synthesis fig-alt="A shared legend identifies solid blue lines as life evaluation and dashed orange lines as emotional well-being across three schematic panels, all plotted against log annual household income. Kahneman and Deaton (2010): life evaluation rises while emotional well-being flattens. Killingsworth (2021): emotional well-being continues rising. Killingsworth et al. (2023): smaller annotations distinguish the least happy respondents, whose emotional well-being flattens, from happier respondents, whose emotional well-being continues rising." width=100%

caption: An illustrative level-*k* ladder for the two-thirds guessing game starts from a random-choice anchor with mean 50, then aims near 33, 22, and 15. These are large-group approximations; the game's equilibrium is 0.
attributes: #fig-level-k-reasoning-ladder fig-alt="An illustrative ladder starts from an expected random-choice anchor of fifty, then gives approximately thirty-three, twenty-two, fifteen, and the equilibrium zero for a two-thirds-of-the-mean guessing game." width=100%

caption: Expected utility payoffs calculated from @tbl-stag-hunt. The threshold is $8/13$, approximately 61.5%; the plotted lines describe this illustrative game, not observed choices.
attributes: #fig-stag-hunt-belief-payoffs fig-alt="A line chart plots expected payoff against the believed chance that the other player chooses Stag. Stag rises from 2 to 15, while Hare stays at 10. They intersect at about 61.5 percent. Below that belief Hare pays more; above it Stag pays more." .phone-fit

caption: Four selected fairness judgments from Kahneman, Knetsch, and Thaler (1986), redrawn from the reported values. A post-storm snow-shovel increase was rated unfair or very unfair by 82% of respondents, and a lettuce wholesale-cost pass-through was rated unfair by 21%. Charging $200 above a scarce car's list price was rated unfair by 71%, compared with 42% for withdrawing a $200 discount. The rows use separate Toronto and Vancouver samples collected in 1984–85.
attributes: #fig-fairness-entitlements-redraw fig-alt="Four horizontal bars report the percentage rating a market action unfair or very unfair. Snow-shovel price rise after a storm is 82 percent, lettuce wholesale-cost pass-through is 21 percent, a scarce-car surcharge above list is 71 percent, and withdrawal of a $200 discount is 42 percent. Sample sizes are shown for each scenario." width=100%

caption: An Asch-style line-comparison activity. Choose a line before imagining that several people publicly selected a different line first. Then ask what their answers might change: private belief, the social cost of dissent, the public response, or some combination.
attributes: #fig-asch-line-comparison fig-alt="A target vertical line of 170 units appears beside comparison lines A, B, and C. Comparison C is also 170 units. The activity then asks the reader to imagine others publicly choosing B before their turn, and consider whether this changes private belief or the public response." width=100%

caption: A norm-message diagnostic separates what people do from what people approve, then tests whether broadcasting the signal could normalize harm.
attributes: #fig-norm-message-diagnostic fig-alt="Flowchart starting with the signal a norm message sends. It branches to a descriptive norm about what people do and an injunctive norm about what people approve. The descriptive branch asks whether the desired behavior is truly common and warns not to advertise harmful behavior as normal. The injunctive branch asks whether approval is true and relevant. Both end in a backfire test for accuracy, locality, independent evidence, privacy, normalization, shame, and uncertainty." width="92%"

caption: Public behavior can influence through two distinct routes. Informational inference can create a cascade without dissent costs; normative pressure can create public conformity without changing private belief. Private estimates, anonymous input, traceable evidence, protected dissent, and support for the first dissenter can preserve independence before discussion.
attributes: #fig-social-pathways fig-alt="Two parallel paths begin with others' public actions. The informational route moves through inferred evidence to possible belief or action updating. The normative route moves through anticipated approval or sanction to public conformity. Both can produce more public actions, with feedback returning to the initial public-action box."

caption: Illustrative Music Lab menus; song names and counts are invented.
attributes: #fig-cultural-market-study-redraw fig-alt="Illustrative menus using six invented song names and counts. Experiment 1 contrasts randomly ordered three-column grids without and with download counts. Experiment 2 contrasts a randomly ordered list without counts against a list sorted by its social world's downloads. Actual participants chose from 48 songs." .phone-fit

caption: Matching postures in a family photograph illustrate behavioral similarity.
attributes: #fig-personal-mimicry-crossed-arms fig-alt="A young child and an adult stand several metres apart on a cobblestone street with matching crossed-arm postures." width="42%"

caption: Reported actions per minute in Chartrand and Bargh’s (1999) first experiment (N = 35). Participants rubbed their faces significantly more with a face-rubbing partner; the predicted foot-shaking contrast was only marginal, p = .06.
attributes: #fig-mimicry-study-redraw fig-alt="A zero-origin grouped bar chart reports actions per minute for 35 participants. Face rubbing is 0.57 with a face-rubbing partner and 0.35 with a foot-shaking partner, a statistically significant contrast. Foot shaking is 0.45 with a face-rubbing partner and 0.73 with a foot-shaking partner, a marginal contrast with p equal to point zero six."

caption: If you saw this €20 note on the ground, would you pick it up—and how long would such an obvious opportunity remain?
attributes: #fig-finance-euro-efficiency fig-alt="A twenty-euro note lies on pavement." width=55%

caption: S&P 500 around the 14:00 Federal Reserve announcement on September 18, 2013. The published minute-by-minute chart shows rapid repricing within seconds. Source: McKinsey Global Institute (2013), Exhibit 12, p. 25; underlying attribution: Bloomberg and Wall Street Journal.
attributes: #fig-finance-fed-announcement fig-alt="The S&P 500 fluctuates before 14:00, rises sharply at the Fed announcement, and remains higher afterward. Opening and closing values are 1,705.48 and 1,725.52." width=100%

caption: S&P 500 futures on September 11, 2001. An initial fall and recovery are followed by a much sharper decline around the second impact. Dashed lines mark the two impact times in US Eastern time. Event times follow the 9/11 Commission (2004). Source: Siegel (2008), Figure 13-1.
attributes: #fig-finance-september11-futures fig-alt="S&P 500 futures from 08:43 to 09:15 on September 11, 2001. After the first impact at 08:46, prices fall and largely recover. Around the second impact at 09:03, prices fall steeply from roughly 1,095 to below 1,070, fluctuate sharply, and partly recover toward 1,080. The curve is traced approximately from the source figure." width=100%

caption: Intraday prices of the four principal shuttle contractors after the Challenger explosion, expressed as percentage changes from their opening prices. The dashed line marks the 11:39 explosion. Morton Thiokol experiences the largest sustained decline. Heavy selling caused an order imbalance, halting NYSE trading in Thiokol from 11:52 a.m. to 12:44 p.m. and creating the gap in observations.[^ch27-thiokol-halt] Source: Maloney and Mulherin (2003).
attributes: #fig-finance-challenger fig-alt="Published intraday points for four shuttle contractors, shown as percentage changes from their opening prices. Morton Thiokol falls to about minus 12 percent by the close and has a gap in observations around noon. Lockheed, Martin Marietta, and Rockwell recover part of their initial declines and end about 1 to 5 percent below their opening prices." width=100% .wide-illustration

caption: Cumulative average excess returns around earnings announcements. Stocks are grouped into ten deciles by standardized unexpected earnings: decile 10 has the most favorable surprises and decile 1 the least favorable. Continued separation after day zero illustrates post-earnings-announcement drift. Approximately digitized from a reproduction of the figure in Rendleman, Jones, and Latané (1982). These are historical portfolio averages, not returns guaranteed to an individual trader.
attributes: #fig-finance-earnings-evidence fig-alt="Ten earnings-surprise groups diverge around announcement day zero and continue separating over the following 90 days. The most favorable-surprise group rises to about 8 percent and the least favorable falls to about minus 9 percent. Curves are traced approximately from the source figure." width=100% .wide-illustration

caption: A possible reinforcing loop links rising prices, expectations of further gains, and more buying. Fundamentals affect price separately, and financing can amplify demand without being required for the loop. Supply, short selling, risk limits, and skeptical capital can weaken the process. Correction can be delayed by funding constraints and uncertainty about when others will act.
attributes: #fig-asset-bubble-feedback fig-alt="Three boxes arranged in a loop show rising prices, expecting more gains, and more buying. A separate fundamentals box points to price; a dashed arrow from financing points to buying as an optional amplifier."

caption: The chart reports 36.5% feedback or momentum-consistent behavior, 33.1% passive or fundamental-value-consistent behavior, 25.4% speculator or next-price-consistent behavior, and 4.9% other or unclassified behavior. Haruvy and Noussair (2006) report 162 rule-based classifications in 18 sessions, with fractional allocation of ties and a highest consistency score of at least 8 of 15 periods.
attributes: #fig-bubble-trader-strategies-redraw fig-alt="Horizontal bars show feedback or momentum-consistent behavior at thirty-six point five percent, passive or fundamental-value-consistent behavior at thirty-three point one percent, speculator or next-price-consistent behavior at twenty-five point four percent, and other or unclassified behavior at four point nine percent." width=100%

caption: An event-study schematic distinguishes the estimation window, the event's first public time, and the post-event window. In the cumulative-abnormal-return panel, positive- and negative-surprise paths share one pre-announcement baseline, diverge at the announcement, and then continue drifting apart. The curves explain the logic of post-earnings-announcement drift.
attributes: #fig-finance-event-study-drift fig-alt="A two-part event-study schematic. A timeline marks an estimation window, the first public event time, and a post-event window. Below, the positive- and negative-surprise paths overlap before the announcement, diverge at the announcement, and continue upward or downward afterward. A side audit lists event time, expected-return model, confounds, uncertainty, tradable timing, and costs." width=100%

caption: The same observable action can become a different social act after identity, relationship, power, norms, history, and situation shape its meaning.
attributes: #fig-culture-meaning-map fig-alt="An observable action branches through four evenly spaced meaning lenses: identity; relationship and power; institution and norm; and history and situation. The branches converge into an interpreted social act, which changes attention, value, prediction, and response."

caption: Monkey, panda, and banana: a three-object categorization prompt.
attributes: #fig-culture-triad-monkey-panda-banana fig-alt="An original textbook illustration shows a monkey and a giant panda above a banana, evenly spaced on a warm neutral background." width="82%"

caption: Mean cortisol change by assigned insult condition and measured regional upbringing in Cohen et al. (1996, Experiment 2).
attributes: #fig-culture-honor-study-redraw fig-alt="An original grouped bar chart shows mean cortisol change of 42 percent in the southern control group and 79 percent in the southern insult group, compared with 39 percent in the northern control group and 33 percent in the northern insult group. A design panel identifies experimentally assigned insult, measured regional upbringing, a between-subject comparison, recruited N of 173, analytic cortisol N of 169, and the restricted White male student sample at one university in the 1990s."

caption: Message design can address obstacles involving attention, evidence, meaning, or efficacy, with belief revision, intention, and action as distinct outcomes.
attributes: #fig-persuasion-update fig-alt="An audience model connects to message design and then to separate outcomes: belief revision, intention, and action." .phone-fit

caption: Motivation and ability to evaluate a message jointly shape elaboration. The quadrants summarize continuous dimensions rather than fixed audience types (Petty & Briñol, 2012).
attributes: #fig-elaboration-quadrant fig-alt="Two axes intersect at the center: motivation increases upward and ability increases to the right. High motivation with low ability means willing but constrained; high ability with low motivation means able but less motivated. Little scrutiny is likely when both are low, and careful scrutiny is more likely when both are high." .phone-fit

caption: Same evidence, different stories. Every panel repeats the same 32 synthetic observations of an outcome over time, on identical scales. Panel A shows the points alone; B–D show least-squares fits under assumed steady, accelerating, and tapering trend shapes.
attributes: #fig-model-underdetermination fig-alt="Four panels contain identical scattered observations with an overall upward pattern. Time increases from left to right and the outcome from bottom to top. The first panel shows only points. The others show least-squares fits of a straight rising line, an accelerating curve, and a tapering curve. No points or axis scales change between panels." .phone-fit width=100%

caption: Mean donations from a $5 payment in Small et al. (2007), Study 3 (159 participants). The identifiable-child condition exceeded both alternatives; the two lower means were not statistically distinguished. This comparison measures giving, not the quality of resource allocation.
attributes: #fig-donation-information fig-alt="Mean donations were $2.38 for the identifiable child alone, $1.14 for statistics alone, and $1.43 for the combined appeal." .phone-fit

caption: An utterance permits several interpretations. Context supplies evidence, while grounding and repair make those interpretations mutually testable. Grounding theory explains this process of testing and repair.
attributes: #fig-communication-iceberg fig-alt="The accountability message may mean clarifying responsibility or assigning blame. Tone, history, and setting offer clues. Grounding means asking and checking: a concrete question and correction can revise the interpretation." .phone-fit

caption: Grounding gives participants ways to check and repair interpretations, seeking enough shared understanding for the purpose of the exchange.
attributes: #fig-communication-grounding fig-alt="Two people exchange words and signals, then use grounding and repair in a feedback loop." .phone-fit

caption: In a task involving 29 dyads, senders predicted high decoding accuracy and receivers judged themselves highly accurate; actual accuracy was lower, especially in email (Kruger et al., 2005, Study 2). Plotted percentages are approximate. The companion schematic contrasts private perspective-taking with perspective-getting through questions and verification (Eyal et al., 2018).
attributes: #fig-communication-calibration-evidence fig-alt="Two-panel figure. A grouped bar chart shows approximate sender forecasts, receiver judgments of their accuracy, and actual tone-decoding accuracy for email and voice in Kruger and colleagues' Study 2. A flow diagram contrasts imagining another person's perspective, which risks projection, with asking, listening, and verifying, which creates a correctable model." width=95%

caption: Beliefs about behavioral “tells” exceed the observed associations for several behaviors. Positive values indicate more of a behavior during deception, observed or believed according to the series. Across nine observed correlations, the largest absolute value is .19; several estimates are heterogeneous. Seven pairs of belief estimates are available, with none reported for nodding or hand movements. Sporer and Schwandt (2007, Figure 1) report the observed associations; their belief estimates came from Zuckerman et al. (1981) and Köhnken (1988).
attributes: #fig-lie-cues-belief-gap fig-alt="A dot plot reproduces nine observed meta-analytic correlations for nonverbal behaviors and, where the source reports them, belief effect sizes for students and professionals. Observed correlations range from minus point one nine to point zero six. Beliefs are often much larger, especially for adaptor, foot and leg, gaze-aversion, blinking, and illustrator cues. The source comparison reports no belief estimates for nodding or hand movements, which are explicitly marked as unavailable." width="96%"

caption: Intent, behavior, and experienced impact are three distinct parts of an interaction. The recipient's response begins the next turn, with the roles reversed.
attributes: #fig-intent-behavior-impact-cycle fig-alt="Four boxes form a cycle from private intent to observable behavior, experienced impact, and next response. The response begins another turn in which the recipient becomes the actor." width=92%

caption: A repair procedure moves from the event and private interpretation toward perspective-getting and a shared next action.
attributes: #fig-conversation-repair fig-alt="Three moves: describe what happened, check the interpretation, and agree what happens next." .phone-fit

caption: Negotiation links each party’s alternatives and priorities to a jointly designed agreement space.
attributes: #fig-negotiation-architecture fig-alt="Party A and Party B each bring a best no-deal option, or BATNA, a walk-away reservation value, interests, priorities, and constraints. They exchange information and shape a process for an agreement where value can be claimed and created."

caption: A positive zone of possible agreement (ZOPA) exists when the buyer’s maximum exceeds the seller’s minimum; the overlap is the bargaining surplus. If the buyer’s maximum were below the seller’s minimum, tactics alone could not create agreement: the parties would need to add issues or walk away.
attributes: #fig-zopa fig-alt="Number line showing seller reservation at 8,000 euros, buyer reservation at 10,000 euros, and a 2,000-euro zone between them." .phone-fit

caption: A first-offer information matrix treats opening as a joint decision about anchoring and disclosure.
attributes: #fig-first-offer-information-matrix fig-alt="Two-by-two matrix crossing your information, good or weak, with the counterpart's information, weak or good. Good-good suggests considering an ambitious justified opening; weak-good says learn before revealing; good-weak says anchor with restraint; weak-weak says research before centering an arbitrary number. Each cell names a risk." width="92%" .phone-fit

caption: Separating territorial sovereignty from security arrangements creates options that a single territorial line conceals.
attributes: #fig-camp-david-two-issue fig-alt="A single-issue frame contrasts Israel retaining territorial control with Egypt recovering it. Two issue cards separate Egyptian territorial sovereignty from security arrangements addressing Israeli concerns. The package combines the issues instead of requiring a compromise along one territorial line." style="width:100%;min-width:0;max-width:100%;max-height:none;height:auto;"

caption: Creating value improves both parties' outcomes; claiming value changes their division along the Pareto frontier. A schematic feasible set with each party's value scaled from 0 to 100.
attributes: #fig-pareto .phone-fit fig-alt="A square plot has value to the seller on the horizontal axis and value to the buyer on the vertical axis, both from 0 to 100. A downward-curving Pareto frontier bounds the shaded feasible agreements. A creating-value arrow moves northeast from an interior agreement to the frontier, improving both outcomes. A two-headed claiming-value arrow follows the frontier: more for one party means less for the other."

caption: MPharm's net payoffs under two hypothetical contracts, before effort costs. Approval adds no payoff under package D but $20 million under package E.
attributes: #fig-contract-state-payoffs fig-alt="Four bars compare MPharm's net payoff before effort costs: package D gives 30 million dollars without approval and 30 million with approval; package E gives 18 million without approval and 38 million with approval." .phone-fit

caption: Vaccination at free workplace clinics (Milkman et al., 2011). Bars show raw rates for reminder-only employees (n = 1,268) and employees prompted to plan (n = 1,270). The adjusted effect was 4.2 percentage points (95% CI 0.5–7.8), distinct from the 4.0-point raw difference.
attributes: #fig-vaccination-plans fig-alt="Two bars show workplace vaccination rates of 33.1 percent with a reminder alone and 37.1 percent with a reminder and date-and-time planning prompt." .phone-fit

caption: A practical workflow defines an action, finds an obstacle, changes one condition, and tests the result. Review can change the diagnosis; after a lapse or harm, recovery or support may also change the goal or design.
attributes: #fig-behavior-design fig-alt="A vertical five-step workflow moves from defining an action through diagnosis, a changed condition, measurement, and review. A return arrow sends results back to diagnosis." .phone-fit

caption: Over a fixed 100-mile trip, fuel use equals 100 divided by MPG. Moving from 10 to 20 MPG lowers use from 10 to 5 US gallons, saving 5 gallons. Moving from 30 to 40 MPG lowers use from 3.33 to 2.50 gallons, saving 0.83 gallon—exactly one-sixth as much. The conversion makes the fuel savings visible (Larrick & Soll, 2008).
attributes: #fig-mpg-fuel-use fig-alt="A reciprocal curve plots US gallons used over 100 miles against miles per gallon. The highlighted 10-to-20-MPG segment falls from 10 to 5 gallons, while the 30-to-40-MPG segment falls only from 3.33 to 2.50 gallons. Comparison cards show that the first change saves 5 gallons and the second saves five-sixths of a gallon, so the first saves exactly six times as much fuel." width="100%"

caption: Masking seldom-used controls simplifies a remote. Keep the controls needed for the user's actual tasks.
attributes: #fig-choice-architecture-simplified-remote fig-alt="Two generic black remote controls lie side by side. The left has many small controls; most of the right remote is covered with removable white tape, leaving only a power button, navigation ring, and a few large controls exposed." width="68%"

caption: An illustrative action cue within a bundled interface redesign. These generic hotel advertisements show how an arrow can make the next action prominent; they are not the original test stimuli. Google reported higher clicks after combining the arrow with typography, spacing, and layout changes, so the comparison does not isolate the arrow’s effect.
attributes: #fig-digital-arrow-affordance fig-alt="Two generic hotel advertisements show the same offer. The second contains a prominent right-pointing arrow." width="100%" .phone-fit

caption: Dots represent repeated judgments of the same or comparable cases; target centers represent outcomes or accepted benchmarks. The patterns distinguish systematic error from unwanted variability. Level noise concerns persistent differences in judges’ average levels; pattern noise concerns different reactions to case features. Occasion noise adds within-judge variation across occasions.
attributes: #fig-bias-and-noise fig-alt="Four target diagrams compare low and high bias with low and high noise. Separate panels define level noise as persistent differences in judges' average levels and pattern noise as different reactions to case features."

caption: A structured judgment workflow connects definition, decomposition, independent assessment, aggregation, recording, and review.
attributes: #fig-structured-judgment-pipeline fig-alt="Six steps define a decision, separate its criteria, elicit independent judgments, compare and combine them, record a decision, and review the result. A return arrow informs the next process while preserving the original record." .phone-fit

caption: A sound or weak process can be followed by either a favorable or unfavorable outcome.
attributes: #fig-decision-audit fig-alt="A two-by-two matrix crosses sound and weak decision processes with favorable and unfavorable outcomes. A sound process can still meet an unfavorable outcome, and a weak process can receive a favorable one." .phone-fit

caption: A 30% rain forecast exceeds one organizer's 20% action threshold but falls below another's 60% threshold. The thresholds follow from the hypothetical error losses, with zero incremental loss for correct matches.
attributes: #fig-ai-same-forecast-different-values fig-alt="Both organizers face a 30 percent rain probability. With false-alarm loss 2 and missed-rain loss 8, the threshold is 20 percent and moving indoors minimizes expected loss. With losses 6 and 4, the threshold is 60 percent and remaining outdoors minimizes expected loss." width=100% .phone-fit

caption: Hypothetical group-average dropout rates show how baseline risk and intervention benefit can rank groups differently.
attributes: #fig-ai-risk-is-not-benefit fig-alt="Group A has hypothetical dropout rates of 60 percent without outreach and 55 percent with it, a reduction of 5 percentage points. Group B has rates of 40 and 20 percent, a reduction of 20 percentage points. Group A has higher baseline risk, while Group B has greater expected benefit from this specific intervention." width=100% .phone-fit

caption: Local moves produce more same-group clustering in one teaching simulation (seed 20260830). Agents seek at least one-third same-group occupied neighbors. A sweep visits agents once; neighbor shares exclude vacancies.
attributes: #fig-schelling-emergence fig-alt="Three eighteen-by-fourteen grids show the same population initially, after one sweep, and after four sweeps with no further moves. The average share of same-group occupied neighbors rises from .48 to .64 to .68. Blue and red marks represent groups and empty marks represent vacancies." width=100%

caption: Five questions connect an experimental design to the claim it can support. Revisit earlier steps when the evidence exposes a weakness.
attributes: #fig-claim-to-design-pipeline fig-alt="A vertical sequence asks what to learn, what to measure, what to compare, how large and uncertain the estimate is, and what the design justifies." .phone-fit

caption: Random sampling supports generalization to the target population; random assignment supports a causal comparison within the evaluation sample.
attributes: #fig-random-sampling-vs-assignment fig-alt="Target population branches through random sampling into an evaluation sample and people not in the evaluation. Only the evaluation sample proceeds through random assignment to treatment and control groups. External validity and internal validity appear as unboxed side labels beside the corresponding procedures." .phone-fit

caption: Three distinct problems in a randomized evaluation: treatment receipt can differ from assignment, follow-up can leave outcomes missing, and treatment can affect other people. An intention-to-treat comparison retains the original assignment groups; missingness and spillovers require additional attention.
attributes: #fig-participant-flow-threats fig-alt="Three panels name and explain noncompliance, attrition, and spillovers or interference. Noncompliance separates treatment assigned from treatment received; attrition separates randomized participants from those whose outcomes are observed; spillovers connect one person's treatment to another person's outcome. A fourth panel defines intention-to-treat as comparison by original assignment and states that it does not itself resolve attrition or spillovers." .phone-fit

caption: Selection can occur throughout research, from the questions investigated to the findings readers encounter.
attributes: #fig-selected-evidence-pipeline fig-alt="Five vertical stages identify question selection, design, data, analysis and reporting, and publication. Their questions ask what is investigated, measured, recorded, reported, and made available to readers." .phone-fit

caption: Selective reporting inflates the visible mean in this teaching simulation. Both histograms use the same scales; bar heights are percentages within the displayed set of studies. Dashed lines mark the true effect of 0.20 standard deviations.
attributes: #fig-selected-literature-simulation fig-alt="Two histograms compare all 2,000 simulated estimates with the 328 whose two-sided p-values are below .05. Their means are .202 and .490 standard deviations; the true effect is .20. The shared horizontal scale shows effect size, and the vertical scale shows the percentage of studies in each bin."

caption: The hollow-face illusion contrasts a rotating face-shaped mask with a featureless hollow surface.
attributes: Raw HTML figure; HTML-only animated GIF
